newsitem.title: USA: GFOA drafting safe harbor to ease arbitrage curbs.
newsitem.headline: GFOA drafting safe harbor to ease arbitrage curbs.

text.p: The GFOA is drafting legislative proposals to exempt some municipalities from federal arbitrage rebate requirements if the localities meet certain conditions, a spokeswoman said on Monday.

Catherine Spain, chief lobbyist for the Government Finance Officers Association, said her group may announce its plan to develop an arbitrage rebate "safe harbor" at a meeting between U.S. Treasury Department officials and muni public interest groups set for tomorrow.

Spain said in a telephone interview that the safe harbor idea is an "outgrowth" of a survey GFOA did last year of muni bond issuers nationwide. GFOA asked issuers for ideas on how Congress or regulators could ease arbitrage rebate curbs.

Spain added that GFOA first floated the safe harbor concept in 1987. The idea did not catch on, however, because the arbitrage rebate requirement had just taken effect and "nobody was paying attention to it," Spain said.

She said this year's proposal will be simpler than the group's 1987 plan. "We like the idea of an arbitrage safe harbor, but we are trying to find something that is simple, easy to understand and workable," Spain said.

Spain said under the earlier plan, a municipality would be deemed not to be earning arbitrage "if the average maturity of your bonds outstanding was 10 years and the average maturity of your investment was 24 months."

Arbitrage is the practice of selling tax-exempt bonds and investing the proceeds in higher-yielding taxable securities. Municipalities are barred from selling tax-exempts just to make arbitrage profits.
